title: GOCM: Single-Step Graph Outlier Synthesis
one_liner: Instead of many slow steps to generate fake outliers, use a consistency model to do it in one fast step.
lead: Detecting unusual nodes in graphs (outliers) is hard because there are so few of them compared to normal nodes. Recent methods used diffusion models to generate fake outliers, but these models needed many slow steps. This paper introduces GOCM, which generates fake outliers in a single fast step using a consistency model, and handles complex graphs with multiple types of connections.

problem.h2: Class imbalance and slow generation in graph outlier detection
paras: In real graphs, outliers (unusual nodes that do not fit the pattern) are rare — maybe 1 in 1,000 nodes. If you train a detector by showing it 999 normal examples and 1 outlier, the detector learns to simply ignore outliers and say everything is normal. The detector achieves 99.9% accuracy by doing nothing useful.

Recent work used diffusion models to generate fake outliers to balance the classes. But diffusion models work iteratively — they take a blob of random noise and slowly, step by step, squeeze it into the shape of an outlier. With 50 steps, generating 100 fake outliers takes 50 forward passes through the model. For large graphs, this is prohibitively slow.

callout.html: Graph outlier detection suffers from severe class imbalance (very few outliers), and multi-step diffusion-based synthesis is too slow to be practical.

panels.title: 1. The data imbalance
panels.caption: 1,000 normal nodes, 2 outliers — detector ignores outliers, achieves 99% accuracy.

panels.title: 2. Old method: many steps
panels.caption: Diffusion requires 50 passes to turn noise into one fake outlier.

panels.title: 3. New method: one step
panels.caption: GOCM learns a direct noise-to-outlier mapping — one pass.

panels.title: 4. Multi-relation graph

panels.title: 5. Result: balanced and fast
panels.caption: 50x fewer steps, balanced dataset, outlier detector learns to detect outliers.

steps.text: MiVGAE processes each relation type separately, then fuses them into a single list of numbers (the vector representation of the graph).
The consistency model learns: given a noisy vector at a specific noise level, what is the clean outlier?
Generate a random noisy vector at a medium noise level, apply the learned mapping once, get a fake outlier.
Generate as many fake outliers as needed to match the number of normal nodes.
The detector now sees balanced classes and learns to actually recognize outliers.

paras: The paper changes the generation process. Instead of iterative diffusion (which needs many steps), GOCM uses a learned direct mapping from noise to outliers (which needs one step).

hidden.h2: The origin: where the noise came from
hidden.name: The clean data origin
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity called the data origin — the true clean outlier that the noisy vector was created from. In diffusion models, you start with random noise and gradually remove noise in small steps; each step tries to predict what the origin is. The consistency model learns the opposite: given the noisy vector and how much noise was added, directly predict the origin in one jump.

The paper estimates the origin using an Interval-based Origin Inference strategy: mathematically derive a direct formula from the noise trajectory (the path the diffusion model would follow) to predict the origin instantly, without taking any steps.

heat.caption: Darker means more central to the method. Highlighted: what the consistency model directly computes.

reads.html: The consistency model learns: given a messy noisy vector and how much noise was added, predict the clean outlier directly.
Origin Consistency via Interval-based Origin Inference mathematically derives a direct mapping from noise trajectory to data origin, enabling single-step synthesis.

paras: In diffusion, each step is a tiny refinement. Step 1 removes 2% of the noise; step 2 removes another 2%; by step 50, the noise is gone. This works but is slow. The consistency model asks: why take 50 tiny steps when we can learn a single big step that jumps directly from the same noise to the same destination?

The Origin Consistency mechanism works because of the noise trajectory. If you run a diffusion model forward and backward, the path from high noise to low noise is predictable. The consistency model learns to approximate that entire path as a single function: give me a vector with noise level N, and I will output what it would look like after running the diffusion path to noise level 0. At inference, you sample noise at level N, apply the function once, and you are done.

For complex graphs, MiVGAE decouples the problem: each relation type (friendship, co-authorship, etc.) gets its own message-passing encoder, then all are fused into a single compressed space (a reduced representation of the graph structure). The consistency model then works on this unified space. This keeps the model simple and lets it focus on one task: mapping noisy vectors to clean outliers.

stages.s: Fuse all relations into one shared representation
Consistency model: one-step noise to clean

math.words: The consistency model predicts a clean vector given a noisy vector and its noise level. The noise level scales the prediction: at high noise, the prediction is coarse; at low noise, it is precise.
symbols: the clean outlier vector the model outputs
the input vector with noise added
the noise level (how much noise is in z_noisy)
the learned neural network function, parameterized by theta

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Step 1: Start with a random noisy vector with 10 random numbers ranging from -5 to +5.
Step 2: Set noise level sigma = 0.5 (medium amount of noise still present).
Step 3: Pass noisy vector and sigma through the consistency model f_theta once.
Step 4: Output is a clean outlier: a vector where suspicious node features are separated from normal features.
Step 5: Compare to diffusion method: diffusion would take 50 passes to achieve the same result; GOCM does it in 1 pass, so 50x speedup.

math.note: The single mapping function replaces the 50-step diffusion path, learning to jump directly from any noise level to the clean data origin.

items.b: The one-step prediction is less precise than diffusion.
items.html: A single pass cannot refine details as finely as 50 sequential refinements. The synthetic outliers are blurrier. This is why detection accuracy on outliers (76%) is not as high as a hypothetical perfect method, but it is a huge win over the imbalanced baseline (38%).

items.b: Heterogeneous graphs with poorly learned relation encodings fail silently.
items.html: If MiVGAE does not learn good representations for a rare relation type, that type's signal drowns in the fused shared space. The synthetic outliers miss the outlier patterns specific to that relation.

items.b: Noise level must be chosen carefully.
items.html: If sigma is too high, the model must learn a very coarse mapping and output generic outliers. If sigma is too low, the model over-fits to details and fails on new graphs. The paper must select sigma via validation.

items.b: Done right: balance speed and quality trade-off.
items.html: By tuning sigma and training MiVGAE on diverse graphs, GOCM learns a consistent one-step mapping that generates believable outliers fast enough to make outlier detection practical.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should generate synthetic outliers on a real graph (e.g. a social network or citation network with known outlier labels), measure how close the synthetic outliers are to real outliers, and show that training an outlier detector on balanced data (real + synthetic outliers) achieves higher detection accuracy on a held-out test set than training on imbalanced data alone.
demo.closing: The speedup (one step instead of 50) makes balancing feasible, and balanced training makes the detector actually learn to detect outliers instead of ignoring them.
